title: Boss: graphs
summary: Count islands, check a course plan, time a network broadcast, and move a knight.

steps.title: Count the islands
prompt: A map is a grid of `'#'` (land) and `'.'` (water). Land cells joined up, down, left or right form one island. Write `int Islands(string[] map)`.

It is connected components on a grid: scan every cell; each unvisited land cell starts a new island, and a BFS or DFS from it marks the whole island. The tests include a 500 × 500 map, so use a queue or an explicit stack (deep recursion could overflow).
solution: var queue = new Queue<(int R, int C)>();
int nr = cr + dr[k], nc = cc + dc[k];
if (nr < 0 || nr >= rows || nc < 0 || nc >= cols) continue;
template: {{CODE}}
Dojo.Eq("the example has 3", 3, Islands(new[] { "##..#", "#...#", "..#.." }));
Dojo.Eq("all water", 0, Islands(new[] { "...", "..." }));
Dojo.Eq("diagonals do not join", 2, Islands(new[] { "#.", ".#" }));
Dojo.Eq("one winding island", 1, Islands(new[] { "###", "..#", "###" }));
var dojoBig = Enumerable.Range(0, 500).Select(r => new string(Enumerable.Range(0, 500).Select(c => r % 2 == 0 || c == (r % 4 == 1 ? 499 : 0) ? '#' : '.').ToArray())).ToArray();
Dojo.Eq("a 500 x 500 snake is one island", 1, Islands(dojoBig));
var dojoDots = Enumerable.Range(0, 500).Select(r => new string(Enumerable.Range(0, 500).Select(c => r % 2 == 0 && c % 2 == 0 ? '#' : '.').ToArray())).ToArray();
Dojo.Eq("62,500 separate dots", 62_500, Islands(dojoDots));
hints: Two nested loops over the cells. Skip water and already-seen land.
For a new island, BFS from that cell, marking each land neighbour as seen when you enqueue it.

steps.title: Can you finish the courses?
prompt: There are `n` courses, `0..n-1`. Each prerequisite `{ a, b }` means course `a` must be taken before course `b`. Write `bool CanFinish(int n, int[][] prereqs)`: is there an order that takes every course?
CanFinish(2, new[] { new[] { 0, 1 }, new[] { 1, 0 } })    // false: each needs the other
Kahn's algorithm or three-colour DFS both work.
solution: for (var v = 0; v < n; v++) graph[v] = new List<int>();
foreach (var p in prereqs) { graph[p[0]].Add(p[1]); indegree[p[1]]++; }
for (var v = 0; v < n; v++) if (indegree[v] == 0) queue.Enqueue(v);
template: {{CODE}}
Dojo.Eq("0 before 1", true, CanFinish(2, new[] { new[] { 0, 1 } }));
Dojo.Eq("each needs the other", false, CanFinish(2, new[] { new[] { 0, 1 }, new[] { 1, 0 } }));
Dojo.Eq("no prerequisites", true, CanFinish(3, new int[0][]));
Dojo.Eq("a diamond is fine", true, CanFinish(4, new[] { new[] { 0, 1 }, new[] { 0, 2 }, new[] { 1, 3 }, new[] { 2, 3 } }));
Dojo.Eq("a cycle hidden at the end", false, CanFinish(5, new[] { new[] { 0, 1 }, new[] { 1, 2 }, new[] { 2, 3 }, new[] { 3, 4 }, new[] { 4, 2 } }));
var dojoChain = Enumerable.Range(0, 99_999).Select(i => new[] { i, i + 1 }).ToArray();
Dojo.Eq("100,000 courses in a chain", true, CanFinish(100_000, dojoChain));
hints: Kahn: count how many courses get dequeued. If it is fewer than `n`, some are stuck on a cycle.
A recursive DFS would go 100,000 levels deep on the chain test; Kahn's queue avoids that.

steps.title: Network broadcast
prompt: A signal starts at server `k`. Each link `{ from, to, ms }` carries it one way in `ms` milliseconds. Write `int BroadcastTime(int n, int[][] links, int k)`: how long until **every** server `0..n-1` has the signal, or `-1` if some never get it.
Every server hears the signal at its shortest-path distance, so the answer is the **largest** Dijkstra distance.
starter: int BroadcastTime(int n, int[][] links, int k)
solution: int BroadcastTime(int n, int[][] links, int k)
var graph = new List<(int To, int W)>[n];
for (var v = 0; v < n; v++) graph[v] = new();
foreach (var l in links) graph[l[0]].Add((l[1], l[2]));
while (pq.TryDequeue(out var u, out var d))
if (d + w < dist[v]) { dist[v] = d + w; pq.Enqueue(v, dist[v]); }
template: {{CODE}}
Dojo.Eq("the example", 2, BroadcastTime(4, new[] { new[] { 1, 0, 1 }, new[] { 1, 2, 1 }, new[] { 2, 3, 1 } }, 1));
Dojo.Eq("links are one-way", -1, BroadcastTime(2, new[] { new[] { 0, 1, 5 } }, 1));
Dojo.Eq("one server", 0, BroadcastTime(1, new int[0][], 0));
Dojo.Eq("a slow direct link loses to a fast detour", 3, BroadcastTime(3, new[] { new[] { 0, 2, 10 }, new[] { 0, 1, 1 }, new[] { 1, 2, 2 } }, 0));
var dojoLinks = Enumerable.Range(0, 49_999).SelectMany(i => new[] { new[] { i, i + 1, 2 }, new[] { i + 1, i, 2 } }).ToArray();
Dojo.Eq("50,000 servers in a line, from the middle", 50_000, BroadcastTime(50_000, dojoLinks, 25_000));
hints: Build a weighted directed adjacency list, then run Dijkstra from `k`.
If any distance is still `int.MaxValue`, return -1; otherwise return the maximum.

steps.title: Knight moves
prompt: A chess knight moves two squares one way and one square at right angles: 8 possible moves. On an `n × n` board, write `int KnightMoves(int n, int fromRow, int fromCol, int toRow, int toCol)`: the fewest moves between the squares, or `-1` if impossible.
Every move costs the same, so this is BFS. The squares are the vertices; you never build the edge list, you generate the 8 moves on the fly.
starter: int KnightMoves(int n, int fromRow, int fromCol, int toRow, int toCol)
solution: int KnightMoves(int n, int fromRow, int fromCol, int toRow, int toCol)
for (var r = 0; r < n; r++) for (var c = 0; c < n; c++) dist[r, c] = -1;
var queue = new Queue<(int R, int C)>();
if (r == toRow && c == toCol) return dist[r, c];
int nr = r + dr[k], nc = c + dc[k];
if (nr < 0 || nr >= n || nc < 0 || nc >= n || dist[nr, nc] != -1) continue;
template: {{CODE}}
Dojo.Eq("corner to corner on 8 x 8", 6, KnightMoves(8, 0, 0, 7, 7));
Dojo.Eq("one move", 1, KnightMoves(8, 0, 0, 1, 2));
Dojo.Eq("already there", 0, KnightMoves(8, 3, 3, 3, 3));
Dojo.Eq("one square diagonally from the corner takes 4", 4, KnightMoves(8, 0, 0, 1, 1));
Dojo.Eq("a 2 x 2 board is stuck", -1, KnightMoves(2, 0, 0, 1, 1));
Dojo.Eq("across a 300 x 300 board", 200, KnightMoves(300, 0, 0, 299, 299));
hints: Two arrays list the 8 moves: `dr = { 1, 2, 2, 1, -1, -2, -2, -1 }` and the matching `dc`.
BFS from the start square with a `dist` grid filled with -1; return the distance when you dequeue the target.
